description: Tata Rekavo (which means 'Fire Tracker' in Guarani) is a team from Paraguay focused on developing data and AI solutions for environmental monitoring. Our goal is to harmonize NASA's satellite fire data (MODIS and VIIRS) to create visualization and prediction tools that provide actionable insights for protecting our local ecosystems, such as the Chaco and Pantanal regions, through a scalable model designed to be replicated anywhere in the world.
summary:
NASA satellites have counted fire hotspots over Paraguay since 2000 with two sensors: MODIS from 2000 and VIIRS from 2012. VIIRS sees 3.4 times more hotspots, so a raw record shows burning jumping x2.8 in 2012, the year VIIRS arrived. Tata Rekavo translates MODIS counts into VIIRS-equivalent hotspots and gives you one monthly series from 2002 to today, with a measured error for each value. We tested the method by hiding each year from 2012 to 2025 and comparing our estimate with what VIIRS measured.

The web app answers "Is this fire normal?" for your area and month, in English and Spanish, for Paraguay, Bolivia, Uruguay, Peru and Ecuador. You can rank departments by how far each one sits from its usual level, count fire inside protected areas and indigenous territories, and see hotspots from the last 24 hours with their local time and satellite. You can send one detection to someone on the ground to check, and look up the hectares that burned in Paraguay each year since 1999 (MapBiomas Fuego). A GitHub Action refreshes the data twice a day. A team from Paraguay built it during NASA Space Apps 2026.
details:
Tata Rekavo is a web application that harmonizes 24 years of NASA fire hotspot data (MODIS Collection 6.1 and VIIRS 375m) into a single, consistent record. Initially built for Paraguay, the architecture is already deployed and scaling across five South American countries: Paraguay, Bolivia, Uruguay, Peru, and Ecuador.

What it does: The system translates VIIRS observations into the MODIS historical standard using region- and month-specific calibration factors derived from the Aqua satellite (which shares the same ~13:30 overpass time as S-NPP). Historical MODIS Aqua data is extrapolated using these factors; from 2012 onward, observed VIIRS data is used directly. Sensor outages are intelligently filled using twin-satellite data.

Benefits: Fire managers and policymakers can now compare current activity against a 24-year baseline with transparent uncertainty margins. The system automatically classifies each month as "Below Normal," "Normal," "High," or "Extreme" relative to historical medians. Crucially, it flags fires in "new places"—areas with no recorded fire since 2002, indicating potential deforestation or fire reaching virgin vegetation.

Impact: In November 2026, the system detected 3,030 hotspots (55% of the usual level) but flagged 78 fires in "new places", providing actionable intelligence for early intervention. Furthermore, the platform integrates Indigenous Territories data (via LandMark, FAPI, INDI, and GAT) to monitor fire impact on ancestral lands.

Tools & Languages: Python (data pipeline), TypeScript/React (Vite-based web app), Vercel (deployment), NASA FIRMS API, xarray, pandas, MapLibre GL JS with CARTO tiles.

Key Differentiators: Beyond raw harmonization, we added a "Physical Validation" (Catador Mode) layer that translates statistical uncertainty into plain-language verdicts for field decision-makers, and a regional "Sudamérica ahora" panel that enables real-time, cross-border fire management coordination.
